verdicts.flaw_description: In two of the four cases the measurement date precedes the feeding date: the tomato was 'fed 3 August' but measured 'by 20 June', and the oak was 'fed 2 May' but measured 'by 19 April'. The other two cases run ~7 weeks forward (8 January to 26 February; 7 October to 24 November), so cases one and three record the height gain before the fertilizer was applied.

A named alternative cause reaches every unit: 'The central syllabus doubled coursework's share of the final grade against the previous year, and every section was marked to that central syllabus.' Doubling coursework's weight in the final grade would by itself raise coursework completion in all four sections, so the 6-11 point rises cannot be attributed to the lab kit.

The timings cover a narrower population than the claim: 'Timings cover the runs that stayed on the issued route, and about a sixth of each depot's runs left the issued route.' Roughly 17 percent of runs at every depot are excluded from the averages, and route deviations are exactly the runs likely to be slow, so the 5-9 minute improvement is measured on a self-selected compliant subset rather than on delivery runs generally.

The absence figures cover a narrower population than the cohort the claim is about: 'Absence figures cover the pupils on the revised timetable throughout, and about a fifth of each cohort spent weeks on the old timetable.' Roughly 20 percent of every cohort is dropped from the numbers, and pupils whose timetable lapsed are plausibly the higher-absence pupils, so the 4-7 percent reduction is measured on a filtered subgroup.
